title: In our image (Genesis 1:26–31)
hook: male and female, made in God's image and blessed

segments.voice: Yesterday, six days and a rest, shavat: separate, fill, and a seventh day made holy. Your line was and he rested. Did you find your half hour? Today we go back into the sixth day. Day three hundred thirty-five.

In the ancient Near East, a king could set up a statue of himself in a city he ruled. Carved stone, his face, in the square. It said: this place belongs to me, and I rule here, even when I'm far away. A king's image had a job. Now read the end of the sixth day with that in your head. God has made the sky, the sea, the land, every bird and fish and beast. And then, instead of setting up a statue, God makes a person. Today's lines are where the Bible says what a human being is.
screen: `A KING'S STATUE IN THE SQUARE.` → `IT SAYS: I RULE HERE.` → `GOD MAKES A PERSON INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: First, the pause. Until now, God's commands have run let there be, let the waters, let the earth. Now the voice changes: "Let us make man to our image and likeness." Let us. Jewish readers have explained the plural in several ways, a royal we, or God speaking with the heavenly court. Some Church Fathers heard in it a hint of the Trinity. Either way, the story slows down, as if this one matters differently. Second, the line itself, in the Douay-Rheims: "to the image of God he created him. Male and female he created them." Both. Not the man in the image and the woman a step behind. The Catechism says man and woman are created with equal dignity, each in their own way an image of God. Third, what an image does. Like the king's statue, the image stands in for someone. Humans are given the care of the earth, to rule it the way God would, which the Church reads as stewardship, not plunder. And the Catechism says this is why every person has the dignity of a person: not something, but someone, capable of knowing and loving God. Fourth, the blessing. God blesses them, gives them every seed-bearing plant for food, and then looks at all of it and calls it very good. The Catechism builds on this line. It's at the root of the Church's teaching on the dignity of every human life, from the very small to the very old, the stranger, the prisoner, the person nobody looks at twice. Each one, an image of God set down in the world.
screen: `LET US MAKE MAN.` · `MALE AND FEMALE, BOTH IN THE IMAGE.` · `AN IMAGE STANDS IN FOR SOMEONE.` · `SOMEONE, NOT SOMETHING.` · then, large: `TO THE IMAGE OF GOD HE CREATED HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a face as an image of God. Pick one. A photo on your phone, a person across the room, or your own face in a mirror or a dark screen. Settle, and breathe. Look slowly: the eyes, the lines, the tiredness or the brightness. Don't judge it. Just let the old line sit over it: made in the image of God. If it's a face you find hard to love, stay with it a little longer. If you pray, you can ask to see that person the way God does. The bell holds the time.
Imago Dei, the image of God: Genesis says every human being, male and female, is made in it, and blessed. Today's word.
Your line: made like him. Today, the next time someone annoys you, look at their face for one extra second and remember the line. Day three hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching on human dignity, from the Catechism to the Church's social teaching, starts from Genesis 1:27, and the passage is among the readings couples can choose for a Catholic wedding.

original.note: Hebrew: image, the word used for a carved figure or statue. Latin imago.

trapdoor: what you thought: made in God's image means we look like God.
what it means: humans, male and female, stand in for God in the world, someone and not something, with a dignity no one can take away.
what a scholar hears: tselem, the word for a carved image, like a king's statue standing for its king.
recall: seeing God directly, as he is, in heaven

notes: Douay-Rheims Genesis 1:26 opening ('Let us make man to our image and likeness') and 1:27 quoted from memory; confirm.
The king's statue as background for 'image' is a common scholarly reading of tselem in its ancient Near Eastern setting; confirm it's fairly put as illustration.
Interpretations of 'let us': royal plural / heavenly court (Jewish readings), Trinity (many Church Fathers). Stated without ranking; confirm.
CCC 357 ('not just something, but someone'), CCC 369 (equal dignity of man and woman), CCC 373 (stewardship). Paraphrased; confirm.
howItsDone: Genesis 1:26–28, 31 is among the Old Testament options in the Catholic wedding lectionary; confirm.
